mainTopic: Which doughs count as 'bread' for חלה: pot-cooked and scalded doughs, borderline baking methods, and dough of מעשר שני
overview: This amud finishes explaining why bread made in a pot (אילפס) can be used for the loaves of the קרבן תודה: one might have thought it counts as a 'broken' loaf. The גמרא then challenges רבי יוחנן, who holds that pot-made dough is obligated in חלה. It quotes a ברייתא about מעיסה and חליטה, two doughs made with boiling water, in which the חכמים say that dough made in a pot is exempt. Along the way the גמרא explains why בית שמאי and בית הלל seem to switch sides: the ברייתא is a 'break' (תברא) joining two separate teachings. רבי יוחנן answers that this is a dispute between תנאים. An attempt to prove that a תנא agrees with him is pushed off: everyone may exempt dough cooked only in a pot, and the real argument is about dough cooked first and then baked in an oven. רבא gives the source for רבי יהודה, 'ten women shall bake your bread in one oven.' In עולא's study hall, רבי זירא explains why two borderline baking methods need no question: dough heated from outside the pot is plain pot-cooking, while a torch facing the dough is how most poor people bake. Finally, רב אסי rules that whether dough of מעשר שני needs חלה depends on the מחלוקת between רבי מאיר and the חכמים, a topic that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why the ruling on pot-bread was needed: the 'one whole loaf' rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the earlier ruling, that pot-bread can be used for the קרבן תודה, was needed. The פסוק 'אחד מכל קרבן' requires a whole loaf, and one might have thought that pot-bread counts as 'broken.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says 'one out of each offering.' 'One' means you may not take a broken piece. Here, you might have thought pot-bread is treated as if it were broken. So the ברייתא teaches us that it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to an unstated 'isn't this obvious?' about the ruling that bread made in a pot can be used for the תודה loaves. It explains what new point the ruling teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אחד' in the פסוק teaches that the כהן's portion of the תודה must be a whole loaf, not a broken piece. Bread made in an אילפס is not properly baked, so one might think it is 'like broken' and invalid. The ברייתא tells us (קא משמע לן) that it still counts as a proper, whole loaf.

keyTerms.meaning: A broken piece of bread
It is considered as if it were broken
It teaches us (the new point being made)
The thanksgiving offering, which comes with loaves of bread

steps.confusionAlert: The text begins in the middle of a פסוק. The words 'אחד מכל קרבן' are a quote from ויקרא ז:יד, not a new statement by the גמרא.

phrases.english: 'one out of each offering'
phrases.notes: Quote from Leviticus 7:14 about the תודה loaves given to the כהן

phrases.english: 'one' teaches that he should not take a broken piece
and here, one might think it is considered as if broken
phrases.notes: Because pot-bread is not properly baked

phrases.english: so it teaches us that it is still valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer to the implied 'פשיטא' earlier about bread made in a pot.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying the novelty (חידוש) of a seemingly obvious ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Pot-bread is not properly baked, so it might be like a broken loaf and invalid for the תודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Pot-bread is treated as a proper, whole loaf.

steps.title: Challenge from the dispute about scalded doughs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא in which בית שמאי and בית הלל disagree about whether מעיסה and חליטה are obligated in חלה, and they seem to switch sides between the two cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: For מעיסה, בית שמאי exempt it and בית הלל obligate it. For חליטה, בית שמאי obligate it and בית הלל exempt it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a challenge (מיתיבי) against רבי יוחנן by quoting a ברייתא about doughs prepared with boiling water. This step starts the quote. The key line is the חכמים's ruling in step 6, and the challenge itself is stated in step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא presents two kinds of scalded dough and records opposite rulings: in מעיסה בית הלל obligate, and in חליטה בית הלל exempt. This ברייתא will end with the חכמים saying pot-made dough is exempt, which clashes with the earlier ruling that pot-bread is obligated in חלה. The ברייתא also raises its own puzzle: why would the two schools switch positions?

keyTerms.meaning: A dough made by pouring flour into boiling water
A dough made by pouring boiling water onto flour
They exempt / they obligate (here, regarding חלה)

phrases.english: They raised an objection: the me'isa — Beit Shammai exempt it
and Beit Hillel obligate it.
The ḥalita — Beit Shammai obligate it
phrases.notes: Notice this is the flip side: on the מעיסה they exempt, but on the חליטה they obligate.

phrases.english: and Beit Hillel exempt it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier ruling that bread made in a pot counts as bread and is obligated in חלה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that מעשה אילפס (pot-made dough) is obligated in חלה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא about scalded doughs ends with the חכמים ruling that dough made in an אילפס is exempt from חלה. That directly contradicts רבי יוחנן, who obligates pot-made dough. The גמרא spells out this challenge in step 9, after a side question in steps 7-8.

steps.title: The ברייתא asks to define the two doughs
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks what exactly מעיסה and חליטה are.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is מעיסה, and what is חליטה?
steps.whatsHappening: Inside the quoted ברייתא, a clarifying question is asked so that we know which dough is which. This sets up the definitions in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both doughs involve flour and boiling water, so it is not obvious how they differ. The question makes sure we can tell the two cases apart before the rulings are discussed further.

keyTerms.meaning: Which is it? / What is?

phrases.english: What is me'isa
and what is ḥalita?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for definitions of the two terms used in the dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact difference between מעיסה and חליטה

steps.title: Defining מעיסה and חליטה
steps.stepSummary: מעיסה is flour poured onto boiling water. חליטה is boiling water poured onto flour.
steps.simpleTranslation: מעיסה is flour put on top of boiling water. חליטה is boiling water put on top of flour.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question by defining the two doughs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference is only the order: which goes into which. In מעיסה the flour goes into hot water, so it is cooked more directly. In חליטה the hot water is poured over the flour, so it is only scalded.

keyTerms.meaning: Boiling (bubbling) water
Flour
On top of

phrases.english: Me'isa is flour poured onto boiling water
ḥalita is boiling water poured onto flour.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference is the order: flour into boiling water (מעיסה) versus boiling water onto flour (חליטה).

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי treats both doughs the same
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי reports that his father, רבי יוסי, treated both doughs the same way. One version says both are exempt; another says both are obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל the son of רבי יוסי says in his father's name: both this and that are exempt. Some say he said: both this and that are obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a third opinion that does not tell the two doughs apart. There are two reports of what that opinion actually was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the first view, where the schools switch sides, רבי יוסי gives one ruling for both doughs. The ברייתא keeps both traditions: 'both exempt' and 'both obligated' (ואמרי לה).

keyTerms.meaning: In the name of his father
Both this and that

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם אָבִיו:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei says in the name of his father:
both this and that are exempt
and some say: both this and that are obligated
phrases.notes: Some people remember the ruling a little differently.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם אָבִיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another תנאי opinion within the quoted ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מעיסה and חליטה are treated the same: either both exempt or both obligated (two versions).

steps.title: The חכמים: pot-made is exempt, oven-made is obligated
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say the deciding factor is how the dough is finished. If it is made in a pot (אילפס) it is exempt from חלה, and if it is made in an oven (תנור) it is obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: for both this and that, if he made them in a pot, it is exempt. If he made them in an oven, it is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with the view of the חכמים. This is the line that creates the real challenge to the earlier ruling about pot-bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the חכמים, the way the water was added does not matter. What matters is whether the dough is finished in a pot or baked in an oven. Since they exempt pot-made dough from חלה, this seems to contradict the earlier ruling that bread made in an אילפס is obligated.

keyTerms.meaning: A pot or pan (cooking vessel)
Oven
He made them

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the heart of the מיתיבי. The earlier ruling said pot-bread is obligated in חלה, and here the חכמים say pot-made dough is exempt. The גמרא states this challenge in step 9, and רבי יוחנן answers it in step 10.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:
both this one and that one,
if he made them in a pot, it is exempt
phrases.notes: This clashes with the earlier ruling on pot-bread

phrases.english: if in an oven, it is obligated.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the quoted ברייתא with the view that actually creates the contradiction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The deciding factor is the vessel: made in a pot it is exempt from חלה, baked in an oven it is obligated.

steps.title: Why do the schools switch sides?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why, according to the first opinion in the ברייתא (the תנא קמא), בית שמאי and בית הלל reverse their positions between מעיסה and חליטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the first תנא, what is different about מעיסה, and what is different about חליטה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to examine the first part of the ברייתא. It asks what logic could make each school switch its ruling between the two doughs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In מעיסה the flour goes into boiling water, so it seems more cooked. One would expect a school that exempts cooked dough to be more lenient there, not less. Yet בית הלל are strict on מעיסה and lenient on חליטה, and בית שמאי do the opposite, which seems inconsistent.

keyTerms.meaning: The first (anonymous) opinion in a ברייתא or משנה
What is different?

phrases.english: And according to the first tanna,
what is different about me'isa
and what is different about ḥalita?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנָּא קַמָּא, מַאי שְׁנָא הַמְּעִיסָּה וּמַאי שְׁנָא חֲלִיטָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to an internal puzzle in the first clause of the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reasoning behind בית שמאי and בית הלל reversing positions between the two doughs

steps.title: The ברייתא is a 'break': two different teachers
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of שמואל (and also רבי יהושע בן לוי, according to another version) answers that the dispute is really the same in both cases. The ברייתא combines two traditions taught by different תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל, and likewise רב יהודה said (and some say it was רבי יהושע בן לוי): as the dispute is in this case, so is the dispute in that case. The text is a 'break.' Whoever taught this clause did not teach that clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the schools do not really switch sides. The ברייתא is stitched together from two different sources.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each school holds one consistent view for both doughs. One תנא reported the dispute using the case of מעיסה, and a different תנא reported it using חליטה. These two תנאים disagree about which school was strict and which was lenient. That is why the combined ברייתא looks like a reversal: it is a תברא, a break between two separate teachings.

keyTerms.meaning: As the dispute is in this case, so it is in that case
A break: the text combines two separate sources

keyTerms.term: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: Whoever taught this clause did not teach that one

steps.whatToRemember: בית שמאי and בית הלל are each consistent across מעיסה and חליטה. The apparent switch in the ברייתא comes from two תנאים whose separate reports were placed side by side (תברא).
steps.confusionAlert: תברא does not mean the ruling is broken or wrong. It means the ברייתא is a combination of two teachings, and the two תנאים disagree about what בית שמאי and בית הלל held.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said,
and likewise Rav Yehuda said
and some say it was Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi:
as the dispute is in this case
so is the dispute in that case
phrases.notes: Each school holds the same view in both cases

phrases.english: and it is a break,
phrases.notes: Here the ברייתא is putting two different teachings together.

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ.
phrases.english: whoever taught this did not teach that.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַחֲלוֹקֶת בְּזוֹ כָּךְ מַחֲלוֹקֶת בְּזוֹ, וְתַבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the apparent reversal.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: There is no real reversal. The ברייתא joins two separate traditions (תברא), each holding that the dispute is the same in both cases.

steps.title: The Sages' ruling seems to refute רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים in the ברייתא exempt pot-made dough from חלה, which seems to contradict רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any event, the ברייתא teaches that the חכמים say: for both kinds of dough, if he made them in a pot they are exempt, and if he made them in an oven they are obligated. This is a refutation of רבי יוחנן!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ruling of the חכמים from the ברייתא. It uses that ruling to attack רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן holds that dough cooked in a pot (מעשה אילפס) is obligated in חלה. The חכמים clearly say that dough finished in a pot is exempt. So the ברייתא appears to refute רבי יוחנן directly.

keyTerms.meaning: 'In any event, it teaches': the גמרא sets aside the side discussion and returns to the main point of the source
A pot or pan used for cooking on the fire
A refutation, a strong challenge against an אמורא from a תנאי source

phrases.english: In any event, it teaches:
And the Sages say:
both this one and that one
if he made them in a pot, he is exempt,
in an oven, he is obligated,
this is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side question about בית שמאי and בית הלל (Steps 7-8) and returns to the חכמים's ruling from Step 6 in order to attack רבי יוחנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that pot-cooked dough is obligated in חלה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים explicitly exempt dough made in an אילפס, which directly contradicts רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן answers that this is a dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says he follows a different תנא, and he cites a ברייתא where רבי יהודה disagrees with the תנא קמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן could tell you: this is a dispute between תנאים. As it was taught: I might think that מעיסה and חלוטה are obligated in חלה. So the verse says 'bread.' רבי יהודה says: 'bread' means only what is baked in an oven.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן defends himself. He says the חכמים are only one opinion, and other תנאים disagree with them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אמורא is allowed to side with one תנא against another. רבי יוחנן brings a ברייתא with two views, the תנא קמא and רבי יהודה. He hopes that one of them holds like him about pot-cooked dough.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is a dispute of תנאים': the issue is already debated by earlier sages, so an אמורא may follow one side
'I might have thought': it introduces a possibility that the verse will rule out
'The verse teaches': it introduces the word in the פסוק that settles the matter
Another form of the word חליטה: dough made by pouring boiling water onto flour

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan could say to you:
It is a dispute between Tannaim.
As it was taught: I might think that
me'isa and ḥaluta are obligated in ḥalla,
therefore the verse states: "bread."
Rabbi Yehuda says:
Bread is nothing other than what is baked in an oven.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: תַּנָּאֵי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the תיובתא by saying that the חכמים are only one side of a dispute between תנאים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute between תנאים: רבי יוחנן follows a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים's ruling is the only תנאי view, so רבי יוחנן is refuted.
steps.terutzMaskana: Another ברייתא shows that תנאים disagree, so רבי יוחנן can follow one of them.

steps.title: רבי יהודה seems to say the same thing as the תנא קמא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that רבי יהודה and the תנא קמא appear to say the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה is the same as the תנא קמא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices a problem in the ברייתא: there seems to be no real disagreement between the two opinions. This sets up the next step, which looks for the real difference between them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא exempts מעיסה and חלוטה because they are not 'bread.' רבי יהודה also says that only oven-baked food is 'bread.' If they agree, then the ברייתא does not show a dispute that could help רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is the same as the תנא קמא': the גמרא asks what the later opinion adds

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda is the same as the first Tanna!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Examines the ברייתא brought in Step 10 to see whether it really contains a dispute.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא contains two different opinions
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both opinions seem to exempt dough that is not baked in an oven, so no difference is visible.

steps.title: Suggestion that the two argue about pot-cooked dough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the תנא קמא obligates pot-cooked dough and רבי יהודה exempts it. That would support רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it that pot-cooked dough is the difference between them? The תנא קמא holds that pot-cooked dough is obligated, and רבי יהודה holds that pot-cooked dough is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to find the real difference between the two views. If it is pot-cooked dough, then רבי יוחנן has a תנא who agrees with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this reading, the תנא קמא exempts only the special doughs, מעיסה and חלוטה, but not ordinary pot-cooked dough. רבי יהודה exempts anything not baked in an oven. So רבי יוחנן would be following the תנא קמא.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Rather, isn't it...?': it introduces a suggested explanation, not a final conclusion
Dough prepared or cooked in a pot
'There is a difference between them': the practical case where the two opinions disagree

steps.confusionAlert: 'אלא לאו' is only a suggestion. In the next step the גמרא rejects it with 'לא', so do not treat this step as the final answer.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not that pot-cooked dough
is the difference between them?
The first Tanna holds:
pot-cooked dough is obligated,
and Rabbi Yehuda holds:
pot-cooked dough is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו, מַעֲשֵׂה אִילְפָּס אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 11 by proposing a practical difference, which would support רבי יוחנן.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's ruling that pot-cooked dough is obligated
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's תנא קמא, read as obligating מעשה אילפס

steps.title: Rejection: they argue only about dough baked in an oven afterward
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Everyone may exempt pot-cooked dough, and the dispute is about dough cooked first and then baked in an oven.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees that pot-cooked dough is exempt. Here they argue about a case where he went back and baked it in an oven. The תנא קמא holds that once he baked it in an oven, we call it bread. רבי יהודה holds that bread is only what was baked in an oven from the start, and since this was not baked in an oven from the start, it is not bread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof for רבי יוחנן. It offers a different difference between the two opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new case is dough that was first cooked in a pot and later baked in an oven. The תנא קמא says the later baking makes it 'bread,' while רבי יהודה requires oven baking from the beginning. In this reading, both agree that dough cooked only in a pot is exempt, so the ברייתא no longer supports רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Everyone agrees': both sides hold this point
'He went back and baked it': it was cooked first and then baked a second time
From the beginning, originally
'They disagree': it names the case where the dispute actually lies

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. Dough cooked only in a pot is exempt according to everyone here. The dispute is only about dough that was cooked first and then baked in an oven.

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees that
pot-cooked dough is exempt,
and here, in a case where he went back and baked it in an oven,
is where they disagree.
For the first Tanna holds:
since he went back and baked it in an oven,
we call it bread,
and Rabbi Yehuda holds:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לֶחֶם אֶלָּא הָאָפוּי בְּתַנּוּר מֵעִיקָּרָא,
phrases.english: bread is only what was baked in an oven from the start,
and since originally it was not baked in an oven,
it is not bread.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מַעֲשֵׂה אִילְפָּס פְּטוּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects Step 12's reading of the ברייתא by moving the dispute to a different case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the תנא קמא obligates pot-cooked dough, so the support for רבי יוחנן falls away.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The dispute can be explained by a different case, dough baked in an oven after cooking, without anyone obligating dough cooked only in a pot.
steps.whatToRemember: In the end, both the תנא קמא and רבי יהודה can be read as exempting dough cooked only in a pot. They argue only about cooked dough that was baked in an oven afterward.

steps.title: רבא explains the verse behind רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: רבא learns from the פסוק 'ten women shall bake your bread in one oven' that only oven-baked bread is called bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: What is the reason of רבי יהודה? Because it is written: 'And ten women shall bake your bread in one oven.' Bread baked in one oven is called bread. What is not baked in one oven is not called bread.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the source in the תורה for רבי יהודה's view that 'bread' must be baked in an oven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in the תוכחה connects 'bread' with baking in an oven. רבא reads this as a definition: real 'bread' is what is baked in an oven. Food made any other way is not 'bread' and is not obligated in חלה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is the reason?': it asks for the source or logic behind an opinion
'As it is written': it introduces a verse
'One oven', the key words in the פסוק
'Is called bread': it fits the תורה's definition of bread

steps.whyThisMatters: The definition of 'bread' decides both the obligation of חלה and, as in this סוגיא, whether the food can count as מצה on פסח.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: Rava said: What is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda?
As it is written: "And ten women shall bake
your bread in one oven."

phrases.aramaic: לֶחֶם הָאָפוּי בְּתַנּוּר אֶחָד — קָרוּי לֶחֶם,
phrases.english: Bread baked in one oven is called bread,

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁאֵין אָפוּי בְּתַנּוּר אֶחָד — אֵין קָרוּי לֶחֶם.
phrases.english: and what is not baked in one oven is not called bread.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source in the פסוק for רבי יהודה's view as explained in Step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, only dough baked in an oven is called 'bread' for halachic purposes, based on 'ten women shall bake your bread in one oven.'

steps.title: רבה asks about dough stuck inside a pot and heated from outside
steps.stepSummary: While sitting in עולא's study hall, רבה asks רבי זירא to pose a question to עולא. If dough was stuck to the inside wall of a pot and the pot was heated from the outside, does it count as bread for חלה?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה and רב יוסף sat behind רבי זירא, and רבי זירא sat in front of עולא. רבה said to רבי זירא: Ask עולא this question: if someone stuck dough to the inside of a pot and heated it from the outside, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets the scene in עולא's study hall. רבה then sends a question about a borderline baking method through רבי זירא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא just taught that only oven-baked bread is called 'bread.' This case falls in the middle. The dough sticks to a wall like in an oven, but the heat comes from outside the pot like ordinary pot-cooking. So the question is which side it belongs to.

keyTerms.meaning: Sat (as a student in the study hall)
Behind him
In front of him
Ask him (a question)
Stuck/pasted (dough onto a wall)
Heated

phrases.english: Rabba and Rav Yosef sat
behind Rabbi Zeira,
and Rabbi Zeira sat in front of Ulla.
phrases.notes: The students sit in rows. The ones in back pass questions forward.

phrases.english: Rabba said to Rabbi Zeira:
Ask Ulla this question:
If one stuck the dough on the inside (of a pot)
and heated it from the outside, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבא's rule (only oven-baked bread counts as 'bread') to a borderline cooking method.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does dough stuck inside a pot and heated from outside count as bread that needs חלה?

steps.title: רבי זירא: עולא would call it ordinary pot-cooking
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא refuses to ask. He knows עולא would answer that this is plainly מעשה אילפס, pot-cooking.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Why should I ask him? If I ask, he will tell me: That is exactly what 'pot-cooking' is!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers רבה's question himself. He predicts that עולא would say the case is simply pot-cooking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heat coming from outside the vessel is the very definition of cooking in a pot. Sticking the dough to the wall does not turn it into oven-baking. So it falls under מעשה אילפס, which is exempt from חלה according to the view that only oven-baked bread is 'bread.'

keyTerms.meaning: What should I say to him? (Why bother asking?)
That is exactly
Pot-cooking: dough prepared in a pot rather than an oven

phrases.english: He said to him: What should I say to him?
For if I say it to him, he will say to me:
That is exactly pot-cooking!
phrases.notes: רש"י explains that the answer is obvious, since this is the standard case of מעשה אילפס.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבה's question by predicting עולא's response.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case is plain מעשה אילפס. It is classified as pot-cooking, not oven-baking.

steps.title: רב יוסף asks about dough stuck inside with a torch facing it
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף asks רבי זירא to pose a different case to עולא. Here the dough is stuck inside the pot, and a torch is held facing it from inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said to רבי זירא: Ask עולא: if someone stuck dough to the inside of a pot and held a torch facing it, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף tries a new version of the question. This time the heat comes from inside the vessel, directly at the dough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The change is the heat source. A torch facing the dough from inside makes the pot work much more like an oven, where fire heats the dough directly. So this case leans closer to real baking than רבה's case.

keyTerms.meaning: A torch
Facing it, opposite it

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף לְרַבִּי זֵירָא,
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said to Rabbi Zeira:
Ask Ulla this question:
If one stuck the dough on the inside
with a torch facing it, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel question that changes the heat source from outside the pot to a torch inside it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does dough stuck inside a pot and heated by a torch facing it count as baked bread for חלה?

steps.title: רבי זירא: עולא would say most poor people bake this way
steps.stepSummary: Again רבי זירא declines to ask. He knows עולא would say this is the normal way poor people bake.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Why should I ask him? If I ask, he will tell me: Most poor people do it this way.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא again answers on עולא's behalf. He says this method is a common way of baking, so the answer is obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On one reading, poor people without a proper oven commonly bake this way. That makes it a normal form of baking, so the result counts as 'bread' and needs חלה. This is the opposite result from רבה's case, because here the fire faces the dough directly. (Some instead read it as the same as pot-boiled bread, which is exempt.)

keyTerms.meaning: Most poor people
Do it this way

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume both of רבי זירא's answers point the same way. In the first case the dough is pot-cooking (not bread). In the torch case, on one reading, it is normal baking (bread), though some treat it as pot-cooking too. In both cases the point is only that the answer is obvious.
steps.whatToRemember: What decides the case is how the dough is heated. Heat from outside the vessel is pot-cooking. A fire facing the dough directly is a recognized, common form of baking.

phrases.english: He said to him: What should I say to him?
For if I say it to him, he will say to me:
Most poor people do it this way.
phrases.notes: So it is a normal method of baking (רש"י).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's question by predicting עולא's response, which closes the scene.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A torch facing the dough is a common way poor people bake, so the answer is obvious: it counts as normal baking.

steps.title: רב אסי: whether מעשר שני dough needs חלה depends on a dispute
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי rules on dough made from מעשר שני. According to רבי מאיר it is exempt from חלה. According to the חכמים it is obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said: Dough of מעשר שני is exempt from חלה according to רבי מאיר, and obligated in חלה according to the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: does dough made from מעשר שני produce need חלה? רב אסי says it depends on a known מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק requires חלה from 'your dough' (עריסותיכם), meaning dough that belongs to you. רבי מאיר holds that מעשר שני is ממון גבוה (it belongs to Heaven), so the dough is not 'yours' and is exempt. The חכמים hold that it is ממון הדיוט (the owner's property), so it is 'yours' and needs חלה.

keyTerms.meaning: Dough
Second tithe: produce eaten in ירושלים in purity
The portion of dough given to a כהן
Exempt
Obligated

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the obligation of חלה depends both on how dough is baked and on who owns it. The rest of the סוגיא will discuss this ownership point.

phrases.english: Rav Asi said:
Dough of second-tithe produce:
according to the words of Rabbi Meir,
it is exempt from challah,
phrases.notes: Because רבי מאיר holds מעשר שני belongs to Heaven (ממון גבוה), so it isn't 'your dough.'

phrases.english: according to the words of the Rabbis,
it is obligated in challah.
phrases.notes: Because the חכמים hold מעשר שני belongs to its owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the baking method to a new question about the dough's ownership status.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dough of מעשר שני is exempt from חלה according to רבי מאיר (it is ממון גבוה) and obligated according to the חכמים (it is the owner's property).
